topic.title: The Translation Index
topic.shortdesc: The workspace file that records which source files have been translated, into which languages, and from which source version.

body.p: The translation index is a workspace file that records which source files have been translated, where the translated copies are stored, and which version of each source file was used to produce the translation.

section.title: Location and Lifecycle
section.p: By default, the index is stored at .contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml.

The file is created automatically the first time the agent records a translation or copies a non-translatable asset. Commit it to your DITA project repository so the translation state stays with your branches and merges and follows the same access-control model as your content.

section.title: Agent-Maintained, Human-Editable
section.p: Under normal conditions, you do not need to edit the index yourself. It is maintained by the translation agent.
The agent also keeps entries sorted and writes one entry per line so diffs remain readable and merge conflicts are less likely.

You can still edit it when needed. The index is plain XML stored in your repository, so you can open it in any text editor, review it in pull requests, and edit it directly when that is faster or more precise than running the agent again. Common reasons to edit it manually include:

ul.li: Force a retranslation - Delete the <entry> for a file, or delete the entire index to reset everything (see Redoing Translations).
Fix an incorrect path - Correct a <source href> or <target href> after you moved or renamed files in the repository outside .
Split or reorganize the index - Add <include href="..."/> pointers to divide a large index into smaller files. For example, you can split it by product area, such as hardware and software products.
Import existing translations - Generate the index from translations created outside (see Importing a Project with Existing Translations).

p.note: If you edit the file manually, keep the format rules below so the agent can still parse it the next time it runs.

section.title: File Example
section.p: Here is an example, indented to be easier to read:

<translation-index version="1"> <entry lang="de-DE"> <source href="../../en/topics/install.dita" sha="b225ce…"/> <target href="../../de-DE/topics/install.dita" sha="08971e…"/> </entry> <entry lang="fr-FR"> <source href="../../en/topics/install.dita" sha="b225ce…"/> <target href="../../fr-FR/topics/install.dita" sha="500c34…"/> </entry> </translation-index>This example shows one source topic, ../../en/topics/install.dita, translated into two target languages: German (de-DE) and French (fr-FR).
Each <entry> represents one (language, source file) pair. Because both entries point to the same source href, they record two translations of the same English file, not two different source files.

The identical source sha value in both entries means that both translations were produced from the same version of the English topic. The different target href and sha values identify the separate translated files and the exact recorded version of each translation.
See the file format reference for full details.

section.title: Resolving Conflicts
section.p: The format is designed to keep merge conflicts rare (one entry per line, sorted, and splittable across fragments), but conflicts can still arise when two translation jobs or two branches record translations independently. Running a single job at a time and translating on a single branch are the simplest ways to avoid them. See Resolving Translation Index Conflicts.
